title: Kaspersky: Retadup worm's revived servers now deliver CoffeeLoader
summary: Kaspersky says servers once used by the Retadup USB worm, disrupted by French police in 2019, now serve a new CoffeeLoader variant. The loader hides in a patched 7-Zip library and uses a packer that runs decryption on the GPU. Kaspersky says its products blocked Retadup infection attempts on about 15,000 systems this year, mostly in Peru, Angola, Russia and Bolivia, and it is unclear who runs the servers.
plain: An old USB worm that police shut down in 2019 is back and installing a newer malware loader that can bring in further malware. Kaspersky blocked infection attempts on about 15,000 systems.
exec: Removable drives can still carry malware that opens the door to later attacks, including from long-dead botnets.
action: Block autorun and restrict USB storage on endpoints, scan removable drives, and hunt for a patched 7z.dll running via rundll32.exe from %PROGRAMDATA% or %LOCALAPPDATA%.

key_findings: A new CoffeeLoader variant uses a patched 7z.dll carrying a new version of the Armoury packer, which runs decryption on the GPU via OpenGL instead of OpenCL.
Domains used as Retadup command servers were re-registered about two years ago and first served SmokeLoader, then CoffeeLoader from early 2025.

Kaspersky products blocked Retadup infection attempts on about 15,000 systems in the first three quarters of the year, mostly in Peru, Angola, Russia and Bolivia, far fewer than the 850,000 machines disinfected in 2019.
It is unclear whether the worm's author or another actor revived the servers.

validation.note: Securelist original (published 16 Nov 2026) now loads: about 15,000 systems in the first three quarters of this year, Peru/Angola/Russia/Bolivia, unknown operator. The Hacker News (independent publisher) agrees on systems, countries and the patched 7-Zip.

review.note: Compared title, date 16 Nov, about 15,000 systems and countries, patched 7z.dll, GPU packer, unknown operator against Securelist original and The Hacker News.
